Read the full description

Tetris meets QWERTY. It's Tetris, except the blocks are keys and every single one has exactly one home. Drop the A on the A. The Z on the Z. You get it. Miss the spot, and that key turns into a useless gray brick that just sits there, bothering you until you explode it. This is game is sponsored by Smart Keys App. Stack them right and the keyboard lights up blue, row by row, until the whole thing is whole again. Stack them wrong long enough and the junk piles to the top and it's over.

Close-up of a QWERTY keyboard, featuring the top two rows of keys for efficient typing.

# Alternatives to QWERTY

The QWERTY keyboard has been around so long that most people just take it for granted. But, as it turns out, many alternate layouts have been developed over the years. [...] The Advantage2 and Freestyle Pro family of keyboards both support native Dvorak and can be quickly programmed with the SmartSet App to support Colemak, Workman and any other layout you can think of.

Because these custom layouts are created on the keyboard itself, and not in the operating system, it’s easy to make small optimization changes for your preferences.

But it doesn’t end there, with SmartSet you can take those alternate layouts and rearrange any key action to create a truly custom layout optimized for your body, typing style, and workflow.

A note about keycaps [...] A layout refers to the arrangement of the keys on a keyboard. If you’ve only used basic, non-programmable keyboards you’ve probably never given much thought to your keyboard’s layout before as those layouts are static. Key positions are determined by the manufacturer and it’s up to your fingers to adjust to the layout. Alternate layouts typically have two goals, which often go hand-in-hand: 1) make the typing experience more comfortable and natural 2) make typing faster. Dvorak, Colemak, and Workman are three of the most popular alternate layouts.

results.title: QWERTYS by Smart Keys by Diegodotta
results.content:
### What you're getting into

 🧩 A Tetris mechanic adapted to a keyboard layout: I thought it would be an easy game, but remembering where the keyboard letters are placed is harder than I thought.
 💣 Bombs to blow up the junk you definitely misplaced on purpose (or not).
 🚩 Flags that flip your whole keyboard into AZERTY, QWERTZ and a couple of others mid-game, re-snapping everything into place, with the appropriate amount of musical chaos. 🇫🇷🇩🇪🇲🇽🇧🇷 (Try tapping the Ç and Ñ for extra points)
 🔥 Combos, row clears, and a 🐢 / 🐇 / 💡 power-up or two to catch on the way down.
 🏆 Spell out QWERTYS and feel briefly, gloriously powerful.

### Controls

 📱 Touch: drag to slide the falling key, swipe down to drop it faster.
 ⌨️ Desktop: ← → to move, ↓ or Space to speed it up.

Stack them right and the keyboard lights up blue, row by row, until the whole thing is whole again. Stack them wrong long enough and the junk piles to the top and it's over. No pressure.

results.title: I tried an alternative keyboard layout... and I kinda regret it 😳
results.content:
### Transcript
[0:00] About a year ago, I decided to switch to Engram,  an alternative keyboard layout to QWERTY.
[0:06] And now I'm gonna explain to  you why I kind of regret it.
[0:13] So let's start from the beginning. Why did I choose to try an  alternative layout to QWERTY?
[0:19] The main reason is that I kind of  had finished my economic journey.   I started with the Dygma Raise,  which is a split-stagger keyboard,  
[0:27] and then moved to the Defy, which is  a columnar split ergonomic keyboard.
[0:32] So I kind of ticked all the boxes. So, inspired by  a video that we did about a year ago about all the   different alternative layouts to QWERTY,  I decided it was time to try a new one. [...] [10:09] It would be in QWERTY and I would  have to look at the keyboard to type. So, do I regret switching to Engram? Well, yes and no.
[10:17] On one hand, typing on Engram is mostly much more  comfortable. Even though I'm not up to my previous  
[10:24] speed, I can notice that my fingers move far less.  But on the other hand, it's not like I had pain on   my fingers before. I can type on QWERTY without  feeling any pain in my fingers or my hands.
[10:38] So, I haven't felt any ergonomic  benefit, if you want to put it that way.
[10:43] In my ideal economic journey, I would  start with a keyboard that is split,   then that is programmable, probably with  extra thumb keys, then I would move to  
[10:53] a keyboard that is either tented and then  has a columnar layout like the Dygma Defy. [...] [9:19] on my Raise 2 and I train it with QWERTY,  I would be able to bring that speed back.   Or maybe the easiest way would  be to put engram on my Raise 2.
[9:31] But you can see the drawback here. My muscle memory while typing is not so versatile  now. I need my mechanical keyboard to have Engram.
[9:41] Luckily, I can switch to my laptop if I  want, but still, there is a constraint.
[9:46] So, you have to be very thoughtful about the   benefits that you're gonna get with  your new layout compared to QWERTY.
[9:54] If I'm gonna grab a colleague's  keyboard, it's a mechanical keyboard,   it's gonna be in QWERTY and I will  have to look at the keys to type.
[10:02] If something were to happen to my keyboard  and I had to grab a colleague's keyboard Please, don't die, don't die.
